claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.
Helm packages Kubernetes applications as charts: directories of templated YAML manifests, a values.yaml file of default inputs, and metadata.
The helm CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
Helm is open source under Apache License 2.0 and the Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Pulumi is open source under Apache License 2.0.
Pulumi derives resource ordering from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.

Helm installs resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind (per kind_sorter.go in the Helm source), and chart authors can't declare dependencies between resources or subcharts except through hook weights.
Helm doesn't let a chart author declare that one resource depends on another.
The Helm docs state: "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's install order is a hardcoded list of Kubernetes kinds in the Helm source (kind_sorter.go), beginning with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-ordered list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and doesn't wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.

Helm chart dependencies don't change resource ordering: a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind, so a chart can't express installing one subchart before another.
Helm chart hooks can be ordered with helm.sh/hook-weight annotations, and resources created by hooks are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
HIP-0025 proposes native sequencing for resources and subcharts in Helm and is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another, or setting the dependsOn resource option, creates an edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi deletes follow the dependency graph in reverse.
Pulumi's dependency-ordered parallel updates are faster than a strict serial sequence.

helm.v4.Chart in the Pulumi Kubernetes provider supports the config.kubernetes.io/depends-on annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and dependsOn on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision, and helm rollback restores a prior revision.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated, and you roll forward by reverting program code and running pulumi up.
Helm favors fast revision-based rollback of a single release; Pulumi favors scriptable control over resources from many providers in one update.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
Two patterns cover most production deployments of Pulumi and Helm together.
The Pulumi EKS guide walks through creating a cluster and installing the operational stack (cert-manager, ingress-nginx, external-dns) via Helm charts end-to-end.
Pulumi resolves output values in a chart's values input at deploy time and orders the chart install after its dependencies.
The page contains an FAQ entry titled "What's the difference between helm.Chart and helm.Release?" with anchor #whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before the ones that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program with helm.v4.Chart or helm.v3.Release is the most common adoption pattern.
Charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering them with helm template and converting the YAML with pulumi convert --from kubernetes.
pulumi import and the import resource option import existing in-cluster resources and generate the corresponding code.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources via helm.v4.Chart and helm.v3.Release, and a program can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private).
helm.v4.Chart renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
helm.v3.Release uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges the objects from a chart and all its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency doesn't make it install first.
Ordering within a Helm release requires chart hooks with hook weights or logic in the application itself.

The helm.v4.Chart values input accepts the same shape as a values.yaml file but lets each leaf be a Pulumi output; Pulumi resolves values at deploy time and installs the chart after the resources it depends on.
pulumi convert --from kubernetes converts rendered charts to native Pulumi code.
